question: Roughly what percentage of waste coming out of healthcare facilities is actually considered hazardous?
explanation: Spot on! The vast majority of hospital waste is actually general refuse. Only about 10 to 25 percent requires special hazardous handling. Knowing this helps us manage disposal budgets and safety better! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h1)

question: Why is it so important to separate general rubbish from hazardous waste right when you throw it away?

options.A: To reduce the overall weight of general waste bins
options.B: To make it easier for administrative staff to empty trash cans
options.C: To prevent clean items from becoming dangerous and costly to treat
options.D: To comply with building design codes for hospitals

explanation: You got it! If you mix regular trash with infectious waste, the whole batch becomes contaminated. That drives up the volume—and the cost—of special waste disposal drastically. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h1)

question: Which of these items is a classic biological hazard you'll encounter on the wards?

options.A: Empty food containers from the cafeteria

explanation: Correct! Items dripping or soaked with blood or body fluids carry active germs that can easily cause infections if not handled carefully. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h2)

question: Even if a bandage or gown looks completely dry, why should you still treat it as an infection risk?

options.A: Dry materials attract more pests than wet materials
options.B: Many harmful bacteria and viruses survive on dry surfaces for a long time
options.C: Dry waste automatically turns back into liquid when touched
options.D: Dried blood explodes into microscopic aerosols easily

explanation: Exactly! Just because something has dried out doesn't mean the germs are dead. Many pathogens are tough survivors and can remain infectious for a long while. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h2)

question: What is one of the most common ways nurses accidentally get needle-stick injuries on duty?

options.A: Transporting bins during morning shift changes
options.C: Using plastic syringes instead of glass
options.D: Emptying safety boxes when they are full

explanation: Spot on. Trying to guide a cap back onto a used needle puts your fingers right in the line of fire. Best practice? Never recap needles! [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h3)

question: Why is a hollow-bore needle (like the ones used to draw blood) so dangerous if you accidentally prick yourself with it?

options.A: Hollow-bore needles often trap residual blood inside, increasing pathogen transfer
options.B: The plastic barrel attached to the needle releases toxic gas
options.C: Puncture wounds from needles never heal without surgical stitches
options.D: Needles used for drawing blood contain paralyzing chemicals

explanation: You nailed it. Because they are hollow, they act like tiny storage tubes carrying a good drop of infected blood right past your skin barrier. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h3)

question: Which of these is a well-known chemical hazard you might find in a clinical area?

options.C: Used cotton wool rolls from wound dressing
options.D: Mercury from a broken blood pressure device

explanation: Correct! Heavy metals like mercury—often found in older BP cuffs or thermometers—are toxic chemicals that need careful cleanup if spilled. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h4)

question: Why do we have to be extra careful when disposing of cytotoxic (chemotherapy) drugs?

options.A: Expired tablets turn into sweet-tasting candy that attracts children
options.B: These drugs instantly catch fire when exposed to ordinary air
options.C: Cytotoxic drugs are designed to destroy cells and can damage healthy tissue and genetic material
options.D: Chemotherapy drugs make the local soil extremely fertile for crops

explanation: Spot on! These medications are specially made to kill fast-growing cells, meaning they can harm healthy human tissue and our environment if carelessly thrown out. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h4)

question: In many communities, which group faces a high risk from improperly disposed medical waste due to scavenging at dump sites?
explanation: That's right. People who sort through open municipal dumps to find reusable items often run into discarded needles and toxic waste without any protective gear. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h5)

question: Among hospital workers, who usually faces the most immediate, daily exposure to sharps and biological waste?
explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you are right at the bedside giving injections, sorting out clinical materials, and managing patient care every single day. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h5)

question: What is the main danger of burning medical waste in open drums instead of using proper high-temperature incinerators?

options.A: It releases toxic air pollutants like dioxins into the local atmosphere
options.B: It creates underground tremors that weaken nearby hospital foundations
options.C: It automatically purifies all the plastic materials into harmless ash
options.D: It causes the surrounding groundwater to freeze solid instantly

explanation: Correct! Low-temperature open burning doesn't break down complex chemicals safely; instead, it pumps dangerous pollutants and toxins right into the air we breathe. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h6)

question: In waste management, what does the term 'leachate' mean?

options.A: The gas that builds up inside sealed biological waste autoclaves
options.B: Contaminated liquid that drains from waste dumps into soil and water sources
options.C: Protective fluid applied to gloves before handling sharp objects
options.D: A special chemical spray used to clean medical instrument trays

explanation: You got it! When rainwater trickles through poorly stored waste, it picks up nasty chemicals and germs, forming 'leachate' that can pollute underground water. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h6)

question: What kind of container must you always use to throw away used needles and blades?

options.B: Open woven baskets with plastic liners

explanation: Spot on! Sharps need hard, sturdy containers so needles can't poke right through the sides and injure someone. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h7)

question: A new nurse is sorting waste on a busy ward. Which action shows they are following safety rules correctly?

options.A: Dropping a used syringe directly into a puncture-resistant box without recapping
options.B: Tossing blood-stained gauze into the ordinary office waste bin
options.C: Recapping a needle carefully using both hands before disposal
options.D: Storing expired medications in the ward refrigerator next to patient snacks

explanation: Brilliant! Dropping the used syringe straight into the safety box without trying to recap it is the golden rule for preventing needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U5_T1#GNS122_U5_T1_h7)
